messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marco was twenty-three when the festival stage collapsed. He had gone with three friends from work, a rare Friday night off from his QA engineering job, where he spent his days scanning code for bugs that could crash systems. That night, the crash was real. The metal scaffolding groaned, then gave way in a single, sickening second. He was near the edge of the crowd and managed to run clear, but two of his friends were closer. One was pulled out with a broken leg. The other didn’t make it. In the chaos that followed—sirens, shouting, emergency lights—Marco saw first responders lifting bodies, and a police officer’s arm blocking him from going back in. He stood there, frozen, watching the news helicopters circle overhead. For months afterward, he could not stop replaying that moment, the moment he believed he should have done something more. He should have yelled a warning, pulled them back, shielded them. He had failed to protect them, and that thought burrowed into him like a splinter he could not remove.

Now, a year later, Marco lives in a smaller apartment closer to his office. He stopped going out on weekends. He avoids the neighborhood where the festival was held, but the triggers find him everywhere. A coworker casually mentions a highway pileup during lunch, and Marco’s stomach clenches. He excuses himself to the bathroom, where the fluorescent lights hum and flicker, and he feels the world pull away, a dissociative feeling of unreality that leaves him watching his own hands from a great distance. When he turns on the news and sees coverage of a warehouse fire, he shuts it off immediately, his heart pounding. He has built a careful system: no television in the living room, a browser extension that blocks news sites, and a strict policy of steering conversations away from anything involving accidents or disasters. He has deleted all social media apps from his phone.

The triggers do more than make him avoid; they also reinforce the beliefs that have taken root since the collapse. Every time he hears a crash discussion, the thought returns: he should have protected his friends, and he failed. He has come to believe that danger is invisible and arbitrary—you can never know who will harm you, or when. The stage might have been built by people who cut corners; the whole world felt rigged that way. And if nothing is safe, then nothing good can happen anymore. Marco has not applied for a promotion he wanted. He stopped dating. He tells himself there is no point planning for a future that feels already hollowed out.

His avoidance strategies are driven by these appraisals. Because he believes he failed to protect, he cannot bear to see police officers—they remind him of the scene, of his own helplessness, and of the official report that concluded no one could have prevented the collapse. He crosses the street when he sees a patrol car. Because he believes nothing good can happen, he avoids any media that might confirm that belief, even positive stories feel like a lie. The counterfactual thinking is the most exhausting: he spends hours imagining how life would have been different if the event had not occurred, if he had insisted they stand farther back, if he had been faster. It is a mental loop that gives him a sense of control he never actually had, yet it leaves him more drained each time.

The consequences have accumulated quietly. His boss noticed his disengagement; Marco was moved off a high-visibility project. He rarely sees his surviving friend from that night, because their conversations inevitably circle back to the disaster, and Marco cannot tolerate it. He spends his evenings alone, running through alternative timelines in his head. What finally brought him to seek help was a morning when he could not bring himself to go to work at all. He called in sick, sat on his couch, and stared at the wall for four hours. He realized he was afraid of what he might do if this went on—not that he would hurt himself, but that he would simply stop existing as a person, fade into the routine of avoidance until there was nothing left to avoid. He is most afraid that therapy will confirm what he already suspects: that he is beyond repair, that nothing good can happen to him anymore. But he came anyway, because some part of him, buried beneath the debris, still believes he might be wrong.
